title: A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools
extended_summary:
This paper asks how effective AI-enabled personalized STEM education is in K-12 schools and which study characteristics moderate its effects. The authors note that prior research on AI in STEM education has been fragmented, with many review studies focusing on qualitative synthesis rather than pooled quantitative evidence. To address this gap, they conducted a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trial studies published between 2012 and 2024.

The intervention of interest is AI-enabled personalized learning in STEM contexts, including intelligent tutoring systems, personalized educational games, augmented/virtual reality tools, and other AI-based applications. The review examines how these technologies support personalization through automated feedback, adaptive content, and classroom or student-centered learning models. The authors also code whether the systems used generative AI and analyze multiple moderators, including school level, AI application type, personalized learning model type, observed outcome type, and subject area.

The meta-analysis includes 32 journal articles yielding 99 independent effect sizes from K-12 settings. The results show a statistically significant overall positive effect of AI-enabled personalized STEM education over non-AI instruction. Moderator analyses indicate stronger effects in secondary school than in kindergarten or elementary settings, the largest effects for AR/VR tools, stronger impacts when AI is embedded in more collaborative or classroom-based personalized learning models, and larger effects in comprehensive courses. Generative AI usage did not significantly moderate outcomes. Overall, the study concludes that AI can support personalized STEM learning in schools, but effectiveness depends strongly on educational level, subject, and implementation design.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis of 32 randomized controlled trials with 99 effect sizes, which is the highest evidence tier in the framework. The study reports subgroup analyses, heterogeneity statistics, and publication-bias checks, supporting strong methodological credibility.
impact_tier_rationale: The overall effect is statistically significant and above the blue-tier threshold (g=0.455), indicating a medium practical impact on K-12 STEM learning. Several moderators also show meaningful gains, especially AR/VR and comprehensive courses, reinforcing substantive educational impact.

interventions.use_case: AI-enabled personalized STEM learning systems classified as ITSs, including computerized tutoring environments that adapt instruction and feedback to K-12 students' needs.
AI-enabled personalized educational games used for STEM learning with adaptive tutoring and feedback.
AI-enabled AR/VR learning environments for STEM, including immersive/embodied simulations sometimes incorporating AI-powered virtual agents.

finding.finding_summary: Across 99 effect sizes from 32 randomized controlled trials, AI-enabled personalized STEM education produced a significant overall gain in learning outcomes (Hedges' g=0.455, 95% CI [0.327, 0.583]). For mathematics specifically, the subgroup analysis found a small positive effect (g=0.398, p<0.001; k=45).
finding.measure: STEM learning outcomes, including mathematics achievement and knowledge/skills outcomes
finding.study_size: n=99 effect sizes from 32 RCT studies

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found a significant overall positive effect of AI-enabled personalized STEM education on learning outcomes (g=0.455, 95% CI [0.327, 0.583], k=99 effect sizes). Outcomes were strongest for knowledge/skills (g=0.603, 95% CI [0.364, 0.842]) and for comprehensive courses (g=2.161, p=0.004), indicating gains in STEM conceptual understanding and problem solving across studies.
finding.measure: Knowledge/skills, comprehensive ability, and course-level STEM learning outcomes
finding.study_size: n=99 effect sizes from 32 RCT studies

finding.finding_summary: AI-enabled personalized STEM education showed small positive effects on perceptions/attitudes and engagement, suggesting benefits beyond achievement. Perceptions/attitudes had g=0.264 (p<0.001; k=24) and engagement had g=0.386 (p<0.001; k=25), both statistically significant.
finding.measure: Perceptions/attitudes and engagement surveys or related study measures
finding.study_size: n=24 to n=25 effect sizes by subgroup

finding.finding_summary: The review included a small set of studies assessing broader capabilities such as comprehensive ability, which encompasses critical thinking and problem solving. The comprehensive ability subgroup was positive but not statistically significant (g=0.381, 95% CI [-0.065, 0.826], k=1), so evidence for durable-skill gains is limited.
finding.measure: Comprehensive ability (e.g., critical thinking, problem solving)
